projections.text: On January 30, 2016, the New York City Council held a 1-3 p.m. hackathon at Civic Hall focused on constituent services.

boundaries: Do not describe the Wayback page as a recovered event calendar listing.

projections.text: The Council described the gathering as its first CouncilStat hackathon.
The surviving promotional graphic uses the branding 'New York City Council Hackathon.'

boundaries: Treat the wording as visible branding, not proof of a longer formal registration title.

projections.text: After the fuller CouncilStat dataset was released, Jamie developed CallNYC.org as an independent public-facing interpretation of those constituent-services records.
Built an independent civic-data follow-on translating CouncilStat constituent-services records into resident-facing issue pathways and next-step guidance.

Built CallNYC.org as an independent follow-on to the New York City Council's first CouncilStat hackathon, translating constituent-services data into resident-facing issue pages and next-step guidance; covered in Politico New York.

supports: sequence from the January event through the fuller data release
surviving implementation of the independent prototype

boundaries: CallNYC was an independent follow-on, not an official Council product, documented formal submission, or winner.

projections.text: CallNYC is an archived independent prototype, not an official or current New York City Council service.

boundaries: Historical officeholders, statistics, categories, and contact information are not current guidance.

projections.text: Working with NYC Artist Coalition, Jamie organized fire-code study groups for DIY venues after the Ghost Ship fire, helping venue operators engage safety requirements directly.

boundaries: Describe this as Jamie's documented contribution within collective venue-safety and nightlife advocacy.

projections.text: Jamie participated in Cabaret Law repeal advocacy with NYC Artist Coalition; national reporting placed the coalition among the groups mobilizing together through Let NYC Dance.

supports: NYC Artist Coalition participation in the Let NYC Dance mobilization
repeal and Office of Nightlife policy context

boundaries: Distinguish Jamie's documented advocacy from legislative authorship and preserve the many organizations and advocates involved in repeal.

projections.text: As a founding-era NYC Artist Coalition organizer, Jamie built and stewarded coalition and campaign websites, issue explanations, calls to action, public resources, and support paths.

boundaries: Use founding-era organizer and direct web-infrastructure language; keep the formal co-founder title in research until independently corroborated, and keep campaign outcomes collective.

projections.text: Jamie translated coalition, policy, and public-data needs into campaign memory, source maps, coordination materials, public explanations, and follow-up systems across NYC Artist Coalition advocacy.

boundaries: This is an infrastructure and campaign-support claim, not legislative authorship or sole causation of Cabaret Law, Office of Nightlife, enforcement, rent-policy, or storefront outcomes.

projections.text: Jamie publicly invited grassroots cultural participants into coalition dialogue about the new Office of Nightlife, arguing that it should protect the diverse community spaces where culture is made.

boundaries: Describe Jamie's documented advocacy and invitation into public dialogue separately from event production roles, legislative authorship, bill sponsorship, and institutional implementation.

projections.text: After the CCED Board recommended $490,539 for KC Town Hall, the Kansas City Council adopted Resolution 190649 on September 26, 2019, accepting the recommendation and authorizing funding-agreement negotiations for an amount not to exceed $490,539.

boundaries: Credit the CCED Board for the recommendation and the Kansas City Council for the resolution; describe Jamie's planning and documentation role separately.
Council acceptance and authority to negotiate are not evidence that an agreement was executed, funds were disbursed or received, or the project was completed.

projections.text: When Jamie's stewardship of KC Town Hall concluded, he transitioned the project to a mission-aligned organization.

boundaries: Present this as Jamie's first-person account unless a public organizational record or collaborator corroboration is added.
Do not identify the recipient organization, infer the handoff date or terms, describe private transition context, or claim present-day project status.

projections.text: NYC Artist Coalition emerged in 2017 as a cross-sector mutual-support and advocacy network for informal and affordable community spaces.

boundaries: Treat the page as a coalition-authored description, not a complete formation history or an individual role record.

projections.text: Within the collective Let NYC Dance campaign, Jamie's web implementation helped turn legislation and public data into a usable civic-action surface.

boundaries: The project artifact establishes coalition tooling; Jamie's web authorship is supported separately by the protected project-history review.

projections.text: The public Let NYC Dance campaign surface combined a Council call script, bill link, district lookup, and licensing, citation, and zoning evidence.

boundaries: This public artifact establishes the campaign surface, not Jamie's authorship or the campaign's causal influence on repeal.

projections.text: Jamie publicly invited grassroots cultural-space participants to an October 2017 Market Hotel town hall, bringing their voices into direct dialogue with commissioners and a Council member about the new Office of Nightlife.

boundaries: Credit the event host, speakers, officials, coalition, and participants; do not describe the event as the legal creation of the Office.

projections.text: The collective repeal campaign reached an institutional outcome in 2017: Intro 1652-A became Local Law 214 and ended the City's cabaret-license requirement while retaining specified security rules.

boundaries: State the enacted outcome separately from Jamie's documented advocacy and from the broader movement's causal contribution.

projections.text: In September 2017, Introduction 1688 created the Office of Nightlife and Nightlife Advisory Board, establishing a formal liaison among City agencies, nightlife, residents, and communities.

boundaries: Credit Council sponsor Rafael Espinal, the Council, the mayor, and implementing agencies; treat coalition advocacy as related public engagement, not legal authorship.

projections.text: Within the collective Talks Not Raids campaign, Jamie's web implementation helped deliver its public civic-action infrastructure.

boundaries: Preserve the named partner coalition and distinguish advocacy tools from Council sponsorship and enactment.

projections.text: The public Talks Not Raids campaign surface documented a broad partner coalition, public report, Council sign-on tracking, and direct constituent calls around Intro 1156.

boundaries: This public artifact establishes the campaign surface and partners, not Jamie's authorship or sole campaign leadership.

projections.text: Intro 1156 became Local Law 220 in 2019, requiring MARCH reporting and adding advance notice and an opportunity for establishments to respond, subject to public-safety exceptions.

boundaries: Credit the Council sponsors and enactment process; describe campaign participation separately from legislative authority.

projections.text: In December 2023 the City dismantled MARCH and shifted to a notice-and-correction approach; that later outcome belongs in the same policy lineage, without being credited to Jamie or any one campaign alone.

boundaries: Treat disbandment as a later outcome in the policy lineage, not proof of advocacy causation; note that other interagency inspections continued.

projections.text: Across Let NYC Dance, Save NYC Spaces, Talks Not Raids, and the archived FairRentNYC site, four campaign press indexes preserve 45 listed references to 44 distinct article URLs spanning repeal, nightlife governance, enforcement, storefront vacancy, and commercial rent stabilization.

boundaries: Describe these as campaign press-index entries, not forty-five endorsements or forty-five articles primarily about Jamie.
Credit each outlet and author; promote article-specific claims only after article-level close reading.

projections.text: Jamie built and stewarded a shared Commercial Rent Stabilization memory system for decisions, action items, open questions, city and state lanes, data stewardship, and consent boundaries.
Built shared operating memory that separated decisions, actions, open questions, aligned workstreams, and protected context.

boundaries: The system supported a collaboration among Action Lab, Small Business United, Fair Rent NYC, NYC Artist Coalition, and other partners; it did not make Jamie the sole coalition leader.

projections.text: Jamie prepared a tracked-change legislative provenance redline that made source lineage visible across NYC Council Intro 93, Fair Rent NYC recommendations, Small Business Survival Act-derived language, and 2025 Albany revisions.
Created a legislative provenance redline so collaborators could distinguish inherited source layers from questions requiring fresh legal review.

boundaries: The redline preserves work by Council sponsors and staff, Fair Rent NYC counsel, prior legislative advocates, and Albany staff; reviewer labels denote source layers rather than personal drafting credit.

projections.text: Jamie designed a privacy-preserving pilot data product for geography-aggregated commercial vacancy and lease-cost indicators, specifying a minimum schema, coverage and suppression table, methods note, and confidential-data exclusions.
Scoped a smallest-serious-v1 for a privacy-preserving commercial vacancy and lease-cost data product, including schema, coverage, suppression, methods, and explicit exclusions.

boundaries: The proposal builds on City data systems and analytical precedents and was developed in coalition and public-interest contexts; it is a product specification, not an implemented or City-approved data release.

projections.text: The method starts with one bounded use case and one approved non-sensitive or synthetic source bundle, then produces a reviewable prototype and a continue, revise, or stop recommendation.
Designed a bounded source-to-memory sprint with human review, explicit privacy controls, and a continue-revise-stop decision.

boundaries: The source establishes a designed method and consulting offer, not a completed engagement, accepted proposal, or production deployment.

projections.text: Jamie helped coordinate and implement FairRentNYC's February 2023 website relaunch through a versioned shared checklist connecting web updates, public action tools, campaign calls, press materials, forms, and follow-through.
Coordinated a campaign-site relaunch through a versioned implementation checklist spanning web, calls, forms, press materials, public documents, and follow-through.

boundaries: The record documents shared implementation with a campaign collaborator and does not establish sole authorship, the full contributor roster, or ownership of campaign strategy.

projections.text: Jamie made artist-residency handoffs repeatable through a documented acceptance and onboarding workflow for proposal review, orientation, space configuration, independent access, and dedicated collaboration workspaces.
Built a repeatable residency acceptance and onboarding workflow, with dedicated collaboration workspaces supporting project and media handoffs.

boundaries: Resident names, proposals, images, access details, and private communications remain protected; the workflow does not make Jamie the author or owner of resident work.

projections.text: Jamie assembled a 20-year working corpus of 81 quarterly HUD-USPS business-vacancy snapshots, organized from Q4 2005 through Q4 2025 for longitudinal research.
Assembled and organized 81 quarterly HUD-USPS business-vacancy snapshots into a 20-year longitudinal research corpus.

boundaries: HUD and USPS originated the government data. The archive establishes corpus assembly and organization, not data authorship, completed validation or analysis, a production pipeline, or agency adoption.
